extracted.intended_audience: general public and scientific community interested in peer review and science communication reform
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and considerations for evaluating and reforming scientific peer review and publication practices, with emphasis on transparency, timeliness, reviewer selection, and incentives for reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review dual purposes: technical quality and journal suitability
rubrics_metrics.description: Often, peer review is being asked to do two things: look at technical quality and determine whether an article is suitable for a particular journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that these are distinct functions. The article notes peer review does a reasonable job of picking studies of interest for a journal but a poor job of improving manuscript quality; reform efforts should treat these purposes separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical quality assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review should evaluate the technical rigor and correctness of a study's methods, analyses, and conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece cites evidence that reviewers miss many deliberate errors (reviewers generally found just three of nine deliberate errors), indicating current processes often fail at this goal. Technical quality assessment may require reviewers with relevant methodological/statistical expertise and different processes than editorial selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suitability for a particular journal (editorial selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review is used to judge whether an article fits the interests, standards, and scope of a specific journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This selection role drives incentives that value attention-grabbing findings (which help placement in top journals) over careful, reproducible work; reforms should separate selection from technical vetting to avoid perverse incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer number and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The fate of a paper often rests on just two or three reviewers, which can be insufficient and unrepresentative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small reviewer panels magnify individual bias and error. The article uses an Amazon analogy: relying on only a few reviews is a weak sampling strategy; broader, ongoing review could give more informative feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer expertise and conflict of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must have the appropriate expertise to evaluate methods and statistics and should be free of personal conflicts (not have 'an axe to grind').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article highlights instances where reviewers either cannot truly evaluate methods/statistics or have personal biases, undermining review quality. Processes should ensure competent, impartial reviewers or make reviewer qualifications transparent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of peer reviews and editorial responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer reviews and editors' responses should be made available to anyone who wants to understand how a paper was evaluated and chosen for publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making reviews public increases accountability and allows the community to see the evaluation process. Transparency is a core reform discussed at the meeting; it can reveal rationale behind editorial decisions and reviewer critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open/post-publication review (community ongoing review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers should be posted publicly before or upon submission so scientists reading them can review and comment afterward, with reviews posted online for the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mike Eisen argues for posting biomedical papers publicly and allowing community members to review them over time — analogous to Amazon product reviews — which would create a continuous, cumulative assessment rather than a one-time gatekeeping event.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anonymity and secrecy versus accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard practice of anonymous, secret reviews reduces transparency and accountability of reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because reviews are usually anonymous and confidential, problematic or low-quality reviews cannot be assessed by the wider community. Opening reviews (or attributing them) could change reviewer incentives and improve review quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness of publication and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The publication pipeline is slow (the piece notes it typically takes nine months from discovery to publication), and delays impede scientific communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Modernizing the process for the online era should reduce delays so findings are disseminated faster; posting preprints and enabling rapid community review are proposed solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive structures: reproducibility versus flashy findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Current incentives reward getting papers into top journals (attention-grabbing findings) rather than producing reproducible, durable work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms (such as public post-publication review) aim to realign incentives so authors are rewarded for reproducibility and long-term usefulness; the article suggests continuous community assessment would favor careful, durable science over 'flashy' results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of peer review to fix pre-study design flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review cannot retroactively fix fundamental experimental design problems, such as inadequate sample size or lack of power, which must be addressed before the study is conducted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citing NIH official Michael Lauer, the article stresses that questions like 'how many people or animals should be included' need to be asked prior to starting experiments; transparency alone cannot solve poor pre-study design decisions.
